fatal_errors: The hypothesis substitutes generic refractory high-entropy alloys for the specific Fe22Ni16Co19Mn12Cr16P15 transition-metal–phosphorus alloy.
It conflates high-temperature oxidation resistance with glass-forming ability; formation of a protective oxide film is not evidence of amorphization or suppression of crystallization.
The cited evidence supports improved oxidation resistance from Al, Cr, and Si, but makes no supported claim that these additions enhance glass-forming ability.
It omits the relevant compositional intervention: adjustment of Fe/Co/Mn ratios and reduction of phosphorus from 20 to 15 at.%.
It omits the essential processing boundary that complete amorphization was achieved only in approximately 20 micrometer ribbons melt-spun at 40 m/s.
The proposed falsification experiment cannot establish the claimed mechanism because oxide-film thickness is not a discriminating measure of glass formation.
explanation: The response addresses glass-forming ability only at a superficial level and otherwise concerns an unrelated oxidation-resistance strategy. The target identifies Fe22Ni16Co19Mn12Cr16P15 as the relevant material and attributes improved eutectic dominance to Fe/Co/Mn/P compositional adjustment, while rapid melt spinning suppresses segregation and phosphide nucleation to produce a fully amorphous ribbon. Appropriate evidence would include XRD, DSC, thermography, and SEM/EDS comparisons between the ingot and melt-spun ribbon. The cited passage instead supports dense oxide formation and high-temperature oxidation resistance, so it does not validate the proposed glass-formation mechanism or outcome.
